# Notes on Acts 27:23–44

These notes cover every verse except v. 29, where nothing useful turned up. Some sources are still missing. My research tools ran out before I could read the rest of Enduring Word (the page stopped at v. 29), Benson's Methodist commentary (the page didn't load), netbible.org, and the Wesley, Lutheran, Pentecostal and Orthodox sites. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage, so that part is left out.

## Part 1: Verse by verse (the traditional reading)

**v. 23**
- Guzik says this was an angel, not Jesus himself as in Acts 23:11. God spoke to Paul in different ways at different times. Paul draws comfort from the fact that he belongs to God and serves Him. That doesn't mean life will be easy, but it does mean God is watching over him even in disaster. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown link "whose I am" to 1 Corinthians 6:19–20. They take "whom I serve" to mean worship or religious devotion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_027.cfm

**v. 24**
- Guzik says "Do not be afraid" shows Paul really needed reassurance, because doubt comes easily in a storm. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- Several writers say "granted you" means Paul had been praying for everyone on board:
  - Guzik: Paul prayed for believers and unbelievers alike. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
  - Coffman: it is a glimpse of Paul's character. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/27-22.html
  - JFB: while the crew worked the pumps, Paul was "wrestling in prayer" for everyone. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_027.cfm
- Matthew Henry sees it as God keeping His promise that everyone would be saved "for Paul's sake." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_027.cfm
- Chrysostom calls it "no slight miracle" that the others were saved because of Paul. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210153.htm

**v. 25**
- Guzik notes that Paul says "I believe God," not just "I believe in God." It is trust in God's word when everything around says otherwise, "not a fair-weather faith." He also quotes Spurgeon on not being ashamed to trust God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- The Biblical Illustrator says God's character gives the believer confidence in His word. It adds that God had said they would be saved "if they obeyed His will." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-27.html

**v. 26**
- Guzik calls this mixed news: running aground here means shipwreck. "A certain island" shows God didn't tell Paul everything, so Paul had to trust God with the details. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- Chrysostom says Paul spoke this as prophecy, not as a guess. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210153.htm

**v. 27**
- MacArthur explains that the sailors heard the surf pounding, which told them land was close. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/1800/pauls-journey-to-rome-part-2

**v. 28**
- The ESV footnotes put 20 fathoms at about 120 feet and 15 fathoms at about 90 feet. A fathom was roughly 6 feet. https://biblehub.com/esv/acts/27.htm

**v. 30**
- Matthew Henry calls the sailors' plan the "basest fraud," because they were the ones responsible for the ship. Everyone else was fooled by their excuse about the anchors; only Paul saw through it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_027.cfm
- Chrysostom says the sailors tried to escape because they didn't believe what Paul had said. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210153.htm

**v. 31**
- Barnes: the promise was certain, but that didn't rule out using proper means, and the soldiers couldn't sail the ship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/27-31.htm
- Matthew Henry: the God who decided they would be saved also decided how, through these sailors. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_027.cfm
- Guzik gives two reasons: the passengers needed the crew's skill, and God's promise probably assumed they all stayed together. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- Ellicott: from a human point of view, landsmen couldn't handle a big ship, so the sailors were essential. https://biblehub.com/acts/27-31.htm
- Chrysostom: Paul said this to hold the sailors back, so the prophecy wouldn't fail. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210153.htm

**v. 32**
- A Bible.org note points out the soldiers could have taken the lifeboat for themselves, but did exactly what Paul said. https://bible.org/seriespage/34-shipwreck-acts-271-44
- Chrysostom notes the centurion obeyed so fully that he let the boat be lost. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210153.htm

**vv. 33–34**
- Precept Austin points out that Paul encouraged them three times (vv. 22, 25, 34): twice not to give up and once to eat. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-27-commentary
- Guzik, on the earlier fasting (v. 21), says it wasn't religious fasting. It was probably spoiled food and seasickness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- The ESV footnote offers "for your deliverance" as another way to translate v. 34. https://biblehub.com/esv/acts/27.htm

**v. 35** (see Part 2 for the debate)
- Ellicott: giving thanks at meals was a normal practice of devout Jews, and probably new to the pagan sailors. https://biblehub.com/acts/27-35.htm
- JFB: Paul's public thanks was a witness to his God in front of everyone. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_027.cfm
- Gill: this followed the Jewish custom that the one who gives thanks breaks the bread and eats first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/27-35.htm
- Bengel calls it "a public confession of the Lord," with the power of example. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/27-35.htm

**v. 36**
- The Light of Israel commentary says Paul gave thanks in the Jewish way, and then he and the crew ate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/27-37.html
- Matthew Henry pictures Paul laying the table himself when no one else had the heart to, and eating whether they joined him or not. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/27-37.html

**v. 37**
- Guzik notes the 276 included both passengers and crew. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- The ESV footnote says some manuscripts read 76, or "about 76." https://biblehub.com/esv/acts/27.htm
- A commentary on StudyLight's 27:27 page says the number is given to make readers care about how many lives were at stake. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/27-27.html

**v. 38**
- Guzik: dumping the wheat shows how desperate they were. It was the last of the main cargo. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

**v. 39**
- JFB: it isn't strange that the sailors didn't recognize the land. The spot was far from the main harbor, had no landmarks, and heavy rain would have blurred the coast. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_027.cfm

**v. 40**
- Chrysostom: they gave the ship to the wind and headed for shore. He says this shows them "do their part as men," and Paul didn't stop them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210153.htm

**v. 41**
- The ESV footnote: "sandbar" could also be "sandbank" or "crosscurrent." The Greek literally means "place between two seas." https://biblehub.com/esv/acts/27.htm
- Matthew Henry wonders whether the sailors ran aground on purpose or God overruled their efforts to fulfil Paul's word. Wrecking with the shore in sight teaches "never to be secure." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_027.cfm
- Chrysostom: the ship broke up in daylight, so they weren't overcome with terror and could see the prophecy come true. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210153.htm

**v. 42**
- Chrysostom: here the devil tries again to block the prophecy. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210153.htm
- The Biblical Illustrator calls the soldiers ungrateful, since Paul had just saved their lives. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-27.html

**v. 43**
- Guzik: God gave Paul favor with the centurion, and that favor kept all the prisoners alive, fulfilling v. 24. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- JFB: Paul must have had great influence over the centurion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_027.cfm
- Chrysostom sees here another sense in which the prisoners were "given to Paul." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210153.htm

**v. 44**
- Matthew Henry: this fulfils God's specific promise that everyone would be saved for Paul's sake. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_027.cfm
- The Light of Israel commentary says all 276 reached shore. It quotes the scholar Ramsay that the front of the ship held together until everyone got off. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/27-44.html
- Fortner (StudyLight): it happened "exactly as God had ordained." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/27-27.html

## Part 2: Where traditions differ

**v. 31: God's sure promise vs. "unless these men remain"**

This is mostly a difference of emphasis, not an open quarrel.
- **Calvinist reading (decree):**
  - Gill denies the promise was conditional. He says the sailors staying was itself part of God's decree, and the means were as fixed as the outcome. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/27-31.htm
  - The Geneva Bible notes say God's promises don't depend on secondary causes, but people who refuse the means God offers make themselves unworthy of His kindness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/27-31.htm
  - Fortner calls the promise God's "sovereign decree, immutable." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/27-27.html
- **Conditional reading:**
  - Clarke (Methodist) says God promised to save them "on the condition" that they used every means in their power. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/27-31.html
  - The Biblical Illustrator likewise says salvation was promised "if they obeyed His will." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-27.html
- **Middle position:** Matthew Henry says Paul "speaks humanly," but adds that if the sailors had left, God would have kept His word some other way. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_027.cfm

**v. 35: Was this the Lord's Supper?**
- **An ordinary meal:**
  - Gill says this "could never be the eucharist." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/27-35.htm
  - Clarke says Paul wouldn't hold the sacrament among ungodly sailors. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/acts/27-35.html
  - JFB agrees it was a meal, not a love-feast. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_027.cfm
  - Meyer agrees, since most of those present were pagans. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/27-35.htm
- **Something more:**
  - Ellicott (Anglican) says that for the few Christians on board it was at least an agapè (love-feast). https://biblehub.com/acts/27-35.htm
  - The Cambridge Bible says Paul "made an Eucharist of this meal." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/27-35.htm
  - Older German scholars (Olshausen, Ewald) also took it as an agapè. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/27-35.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Paul's words match Jesus' at the feedings of the crowds. But the words "This is my body," which made the Last Supper a sacrament, are missing. https://biblehub.com/acts/27-35.htm

## Part 3: Other views

**Catholic**
- The old Catholic Encyclopedia says the setting "altogether excludes" a Eucharist. It treats the verse as an example of grace before meals. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/tce/t/thanksgiving-before-and-after-meals.html
- A Catholic Answers article says that even if it wasn't technically a Mass, the meal "clearly bears resemblance" to one. It uses the passage to argue the Last Supper bread was wheat. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/why-wheat-bread

**Patristic (shared by Orthodox and Catholics)**
- Chrysostom's Homily 53 reads the whole scene as Paul's prophecy being fulfilled despite the devil's interference. He says the people on board were taught by Paul's calm "as in a church." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210153.htm

**Modern critical scholarship**
- Holtzmann claimed v. 31 contradicts vv. 24–26. An older commentary on Bible Hub, unnamed in the excerpt, calls that "altogether hypercritical." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/27-31.htm

**Popular typology and application**
- Bible.org reads the rescue as a picture of salvation: trusting Christ the way the passengers had to trust Paul. https://bible.org/seriespage/34-shipwreck-acts-271-44
- Gaebelein links the meal to feeding on the bread of life in times of danger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/acts-27.html
- The Bible Hub study notes compare "remain with the ship" to abiding in Christ (John 15). https://biblehub.com/study/acts/27-31.htm
